name: Languages (Hebrew, Aramaic, Ugaritic)

objectives.text: Identify that most of the Old Testament was first written in the Hebrew language
Name the meanings of Hebrew words still used in worship today, such as shalom, amen, and hallelujah
Recall that Jesus spoke Aramaic and identify Aramaic words kept in the Gospels, such as Abba and Talitha cumi
Describe how Hebrew is written from right to left using an alphabet of twenty-two letters
Explain that our English Bible is translated from the original Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek so that people can read God's Word in their own language
Locate the passages of the Old Testament written in Aramaic and explain why those sections fit an Aramaic-speaking setting
Explain how Hebrew names carry meanings that connect to the stories and promises of Scripture
Compare how two English translations render the same verse and explain why translators must choose between possible words
Analyze how the Dead Sea Scrolls, such as the Great Isaiah Scroll, give evidence for the careful transmission of the Hebrew text
Describe Hebrew as a Semitic language related to Aramaic, Ugaritic, Phoenician, and Akkadian
Compare word-for-word and thought-for-thought translation approaches and evaluate the strengths of each for Bible study
Explain why Jews translated the Old Testament into Greek in the Septuagint and how New Testament writers quote it
Describe the discovery of the Ugaritic texts at Ras Shamra and explain how they help clarify rare Hebrew words and poetic patterns
Explain how the Masoretes preserved the Hebrew text by adding vowel points and careful scribal notes
Conduct a Hebrew word study using a concordance and lexicon to trace a word's meaning across several passages
Analyze how biblical poets use Canaanite language known from Ugaritic texts to declare the LORD's supremacy over Baal
Evaluate how understanding Hebrew terms such as hesed and berit enriches the meaning of key doctrinal passages
Explain the Reformed teaching that Scripture in its original languages is the final authority, providentially preserved, and to be translated for all peoples
Evaluate arguments for the reliable preservation of the Old Testament text using manuscript evidence
Analyze the spread of Aramaic as the common language of the ancient Near East using evidence from the Old Testament
Compare readings of a passage in the Masoretic Text, the Septuagint, and the Dead Sea Scrolls and explain how scholars weigh textual differences

changes: Kept and reworded real competencies (Hebrew origin, shalom, Aramaic of Jesus, Hebrew script, English Bible from originals, Aramaic in Daniel, translation choices, Dead Sea Scrolls, translation philosophies, Ugaritic, Septuagint, word study, hesed, preservation, Aramaic lingua franca). Dropped the filler letter-comparison objective by folding it into the script objective. Added Gospel Aramaic words, Aramaic sections of Ezra and Jeremiah, meaningful Hebrew names, Semitic language family, Masoretes, Ugaritic polemic in Psalms, Reformed doctrine of original-language authority, and comparison of textual witnesses. Anchored doctrine of the original languages to Westminster Confession of Faith 1.8 and replaced chapter-level gaps with specific verses.
